en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on False Speech, 9.
The Training Rule on Announcing What is Grave.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta had fallen into a quarrel with the group-of-six monks.
Having committed an intentional offense of emitting semen, he requested the Saṅgha for probation regarding that offense.
The Saṅgha granted him probation for that offense.
Now at that time, a certain guild in Sāvatthī had provided a meal for the Saṅgha.
While observing the period of probation, he sat at the very end of the row of seats in the dining hall.
The group of six monks said this to those lay followers:

“Friends, this venerable Upananda the Sakyan son is one whom you hold in high esteem and who frequents your families. With the very same hand with which he eats what has been given in faith, he intentionally discharged semen.
Having committed an offense of intentional emission of semen, he requested the Saṅgha for probation for that offense.
The Saṅgha granted him probation for that offense.”
While he was undergoing probation, he sat at the edge of his seat.
Those monks who were few in desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and were indignant, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks report a grave offense of a monk to one who is not fully ordained?"... [as before]...
“Is it true, monks, that you report a grave offense of a monk to one who is not fully ordained?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before] ...
"How indeed, you foolish men, can you report a grave offense of a bhikkhu to one who is not fully ordained?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Whatever monk should report a grave offense of a monk to one who is not fully ordained, except by the authorization of the monks, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whatever monk” means whichever kind of monk... [and so on].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Of the bhikkhu" (bhikkhussa):
To another bhikkhu.
A grave offense (duṭṭhulla-āpatti) means:
the four pārājikas and the thirteen saṅghādisesas.
"One not fully ordained" means:
with the exception of a bhikkhu and a bhikkhunī, everyone else is called "one not fully ordained.
"Should inform" means:
One should inform either a woman or a man, whether a householder or one who has gone forth.
"Except with the consent of the bhikkhus" means setting aside the consent of the bhikkhus.
There is a formal authorization of the monks that is limited by the offense, not limited by the family;

there is a formal authorization of the monks that is limited by the family, not limited by the offense; there is a formal authorization of the monks that is limited both by the offense and by the family; and there is a formal authorization of the monks that is limited neither by the offense nor by the family.
[Regarding these,] "limited by the offense" means:
The offenses are determined: "One should inform [the preceptor] of so many offenses.
Families are delimited: "One should inform [the preceptor] within such-and-such families."

“Limited by offenses and limited by families” means that both the offenses are defined and the families are defined, such that one must report [the offense] regarding so many offenses to so many families.
“Neither limited by offenses nor limited by families” means...

If the offenses have not been delimited and the families have not been delimited— [meaning] it has not been determined that "one should report [the offense] regarding so many offenses to so many families"—
then if, setting aside those offenses which have been delimited within the limit of offenses, one reports them by means of other offenses, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). If,
setting aside those families which have been delimited within the limit of families, one reports [the offense] to other families, there is an offense of expiation.
If, having set aside those offenses which have been determined within the limits of the offenses and the limits of the families,
and having set aside those families which have been determined, she reports other offenses to other families,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
There is no offense if there is neither a limit to the offense nor a limit to the family.

If one informs a person who is not fully ordained of a grave offense, perceiving it as a grave offense, except by the authorization of the Saṅgha, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
If one informs a person who is not fully ordained of a grave offense while being in doubt about it, except by the authorization of the Saṅgha, there is an offense entailing confession.
If one perceives a grave offense as not grave and informs a person who is not fully ordained, except by the consent of the Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one informs [a person who is not fully ordained] of a non-grave offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If one informs a person who is not fully ordained of a transgression, whether grave or non-grave, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is a non-gross offense, but he perceives it as a gross offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is a non-gross offense, but he is uncertain about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is a non-gross offense, and he perceives it as a non-gross offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if one reports the matter but not the offense,
or reports the offense but not the matter.
[It is not an offense] for one who has the consent of the bhikkhus,
for one who is insane,
or for an original offender.
The ninth training rule concerning the announcement of what is grave is finished.
